outline.chapter_title: Orientation: Minnesota Wage-and-Hour Enforcement Meets Federal Justiciability
outline.description: Introduces the architecture of Minnesota wage-and-hour law and the federal Article III limits that shape private enforcement of state statutory remedies in federal court.
subtopics: Purposes and scope of Minnesota’s wage statutes: timely payment, minimum wage and overtime, and wage theft prevention
Public–private enforcement model: role of the Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry versus private litigants
Article III overview: standing, redressability, and mootness constraints on state-law claims in federal court
Using Cohen v. Consilio as a teaching vehicle for the intersection of remedial design and federal jurisdiction

outline.chapter_title: The Statutory Framework: MPWA, MFLSA, and MWTA
outline.description: Maps the core Minnesota statutes governing wage payment, overtime, and notice obligations, emphasizing who may sue, what remedies exist, and how they interrelate.
subtopics: Minnesota Payment of Wages Act (MPWA), Minn. Stat. § 181.101: timely payment, Commissioner’s demand authority, and employee wage claims
Minn. Stat. §§ 181.13 and 181.14: discharge/quit wage provisions and employee-accessible penalties
Minnesota Fair Labor Standards Act (MFLSA), Minn. Stat. §§ 177.25 and 177.27: overtime rights, liquidated damages, and agency civil penalties
Minnesota Wage Theft Act (MWTA), Minn. Stat. § 181.032: written notice and change-notice requirements
Private right of action under Minn. Stat. § 181.171, subd. 1 and MFLSA § 177.27, subd. 8

outline.chapter_title: Remedies and Enforcement Authority Under Minnesota Law
outline.description: Explains the palette of available remedies, distinguishes compensatory from punitive relief, and clarifies which actors can obtain or collect each form of relief.
subtopics: Back wages versus statutory liquidated damages versus civil penalties
Who can seek or collect civil penalties: Commissioner-only penalties under several provisions
“Other appropriate relief” and injunctive relief under § 181.171
Attorney’s fees, costs, and prejudgment interest under MPWA and MFLSA
Commissioner demand process and calculation of average daily wage penalties under § 181.101(a)

outline.chapter_title: Case Study Setup: Cohen v. Consilio
outline.description: Sets out the factual background and procedural posture that frame the doctrinal issues, focusing on the employer’s overtime policy and the parties’ strategic stipulations.
subtopics: Consilio’s 2019 change to eliminate overtime premium and pay base rate for all hours
Plaintiff’s claims under MPWA, MFLSA, and MWTA; requests for wages, penalties, liquidated damages, and injunction
Employer’s payments of overtime and MFLSA liquidated damages; stipulation as to amounts owed
Issues preserved: statutory penalties (MPWA and MFLSA), MWTA notice remedies, and injunctive relief
Appellate standard of review for summary judgment

outline.chapter_title: Interpreting MPWA § 181.101: Commissioner-Only Average Daily Wage Penalties
outline.description: Uses Cohen to teach statutory interpretation of § 181.101 and the limits of private enforcement of penalties under the MPWA.
subtopics: Textual structure of § 181.101(a): employee wage claim versus Commissioner’s penalty authority
Private right of action under § 181.171, subd. 1 and the clause limiting recovery of civil penalties to those “provided for in the section violated”
Comparative statutory design: §§ 181.13 and 181.14 expressly authorize employee penalties; negative inference canon
Allan v. R.D. Offutt (plain meaning), Lagasse v. Horton (legislature “knows how” canon), and Milner v. Farmers Ins. Exchange (allocation of penalties)
Application in Cohen: why employees may sue for wages but cannot privately obtain average daily wage penalties under § 181.101

outline.chapter_title: MFLSA Civil Penalties and Article III: Redressability and Mootness
outline.description: Explores whether and when a private plaintiff has Article III standing to pursue MFLSA civil penalties payable to the state, and how voluntary cessation and mootness operate.
subtopics: MFLSA remedies: private recovery of wages and liquidated damages; civil penalties available to and collected by the Commissioner (Milner)
Redressability when penalties go to the government: Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw rationale
Standing must persist through the case; Town of Chester and Sisney on claim-specific standing and mootness
Voluntary cessation doctrine and the “absolutely clear” burden; City of Mesquite
Cohen’s remand: factual determination whether the overtime policy remains or could reasonably recur and the implications for mootness

outline.chapter_title: MWTA Notice Duties and Private Remedies
outline.description: Details the MWTA’s notice requirements and what relief is available for violations, using Cohen to illustrate the limits of civil penalties and the importance of developed argument.
subtopics: MWTA § 181.032(d)(4) and (f): initial and change-in-terms notice requirements
Private enforcement via § 181.171: damages and “other appropriate relief” but no civil penalties absent express provision in § 181.032
What damages might be recoverable for notice violations and proof challenges
Cohen’s waiver on appeal for lack of developed argument and authority

outline.description: Addresses how to seek injunctive relief under Minnesota wage statutes and federal rules, and how missteps can forfeit equitable claims.
subtopics: Availability of injunctive relief as “other appropriate relief” under § 181.171 and under MFLSA
Pleading specific injunctive relief and amending claims; Rule 15(a) mechanics
Why new claims cannot be raised in opposition briefs (InfoDeli) and preservation on appeal
Interaction between injunctive relief and mootness/redressability in wage-and-hour cases

outline.chapter_title: Payments Mid-Litigation, Stipulations, and the ‘Pick-Off’ Problem
outline.description: Analyzes the effect of an employer’s strategic payment of wages and liquidated damages on remaining claims, including penalties and equitable relief, and implications for putative class actions.
subtopics: Impact of paying back wages and liquidated damages on standing and mootness
Distinguishing federal Rule 68 and Campbell-Ewald pick-off issues from Minnesota wage claims
Drafting stipulations: preserving unresolved issues (penalties, injunctive relief) and jurisdictional facts
Timing considerations relative to class certification and adequacy of representation

outline.chapter_title: Building the Record and Summary Judgment Practice
outline.description: Offers guidance on evidentiary development and briefing to survive or win summary judgment on statutory penalties, notice violations, and equitable relief.
subtopics: Evidence of ongoing or ceased policies relevant to voluntary cessation and mootness
Proof of Commissioner demand and penalty eligibility under § 181.101
Documenting MWTA compliance or violations and resulting damages
Appellate preservation: avoiding waiver through developed, supported argument
Standards of review and burdens at summary judgment in wage-and-hour cases

outline.description: Places Minnesota’s scheme in broader context by comparing to the FLSA and other states, and evaluates policy choices about centralized penalty enforcement versus private penalties.
subtopics: FLSA remedies: private liquidated damages versus DOL civil money penalties; parallels to Minnesota’s allocation
Other states’ penalty regimes (e.g., California’s waiting-time penalties) and private standing to recover penalties
Policy tradeoffs: deterrence, administrative coherence, and risk of over- or under-enforcement
Coordinating private suits with agency investigations and settlements

outline.chapter_title: Significance of Cohen v. Consilio and Looking Ahead
outline.description: Assesses Cohen’s contributions to Minnesota wage law and federal jurisdiction doctrine, identifies open questions, and offers practice takeaways.
subtopics: Clarification that MPWA § 181.101 average daily wage penalties are Commissioner-only
Unresolved standing and mootness questions for MFLSA civil penalties payable to the state
Practical guidance: when to involve the Commissioner; preserving injunctive claims; evidentiary focus on ongoing policies
Employer compliance lessons: changing pay policies and providing timely, accurate notice
Potential legislative responses to clarify private penalty rights or redressability concerns

outline.description: Applies the chapter’s doctrines through structured scenarios to test understanding and strategic thinking.
subtopics: Scenario: Commissioner issues a § 181.101 demand; employer pays wages but not penalties—who can sue for what?
Scenario: Employer rescinds illegal overtime policy post-filing and adopts a compliant policy—mootness analysis under Laidlaw
Scenario: MWTA notice omitted but no wage underpayment—what damages or relief can a private plaintiff seek?
Scenario: Putative class case where only named plaintiff is made whole—effect on class claims and penalties
